source.title: Neuron-based explanations of neural networks sacrifice completeness and interpretability
source.authors: Nolan Dey; J. E. Taylor; A. Wong; B. Tripp; Graham W. Taylor

page_placements.theme: Interpretable features are not neuron-aligned: each spreads over many neurons

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron polysemanticity as motivation, but its experiments compare neuron- and PCA-based explanations for completeness and human-rated interpretability. They do not test whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, why they might do so, or whether apparent mixtures share a feature.
record.gate_note: The neuron-versus-PCA interpretability and completeness results are about neuron-based explanations, but none of the listed versions directly describes those comparisons. The paper does not measure polysemantic response mixtures or test the cited InceptionV1 neuron. The Zoom In paper is cited as motivation; its results are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The paper cites neuron polysemanticity (Zoom In) only as motivation. Its experiments compare neuron and PCA bases in AlexNet on explained variance, ablation accuracy and a human coherence-rating task. None of these measures whether a neuron responds to several unrelated inputs, why it would, or whether apparent mixtures share one feature. The finding that deeper neuron visualizations look 'semantically meaningless' is a judgment of interpretability, not a count of polysemantic neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. For AlexNet, top PCs give more complete and more interpretable explanations than top neurons, with conv1 an exception in ablation. The authors caution that generality beyond AlexNet is untested and that neurons may still be useful in first and final layers.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses sampled activation-space points, natural-image nearest neighbors, PCA comparisons, activation ablations, and a human coherence-rating task; it does not reproduce the cited Distill study’s analysis of InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability ratings vary with layer depth; the PCA advantage was especially pronounced in fc1 and fc2 and less so in fc3. The authors also report that sampling the full minimum-to-maximum activation range gives more distinct visualizations than sampling the first-to-ninety-ninth percentile.

fits_no_version.finding: Human raters detected coherent transitions more accurately for top PCs than for top neurons in every AlexNet layer, with the largest gaps in conv2, fc1 and fc2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In AlexNet, top activation principal components are more interpretable to humans than top neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation variance is far more concentrated in PCs than in neurons. In fc1, 80% of variance needs 42 PCs versus 2782 neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AlexNet representations are distributed across neurons, so a few PCs summarize most activation variance.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating high-variance PCs usually hurts accuracy more than ablating high-variance neurons. In conv1 the pattern reverses, and in conv4 and conv5 it reverses after about 50 components.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative functional importance of PCs and neurons depends on the layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron visualizations from conv3 to fc3 appear semantically meaningless.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deeper AlexNet neurons are hard to interpret individually.

fits_no_version.finding: Sampling across the full min–max activation range gave more distinct visualizations than sampling between the 1st and 99th percentiles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The sampled activation range affects how distinct a visualized feature appears.

record.problems: The main experiments focus on AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet; the authors state they did not compare neuron- and PCA-based completeness and interpretability across other networks or datasets. The human task tests recognition of a coherent transition, which the authors describe as a low threshold for interpretability. Many plotted results have no exact values in the text. The study does not directly measure polysemantic response mixtures.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out. Cited findings from other studies, including the cited Zoom In work, are not recorded as this study’s results.

untested.parts: Whether individual InceptionV1 or AlexNet neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. Not measured.
Language-model MLP neurons. Not studied; ViT appears only in explained-variance plots.
Superposition or capacity pressure as a cause.
Initialization, regularization or noise as causes.
Effect of activation function, architecture or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons.
Whether canonical mixed neurons detect one shared feature.
Appendix C changes the visualization sampling range, but only for one PC's distinctness, not for neuron polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because no version is tested. Polysemanticity appears only as cited motivation (Olah et al. 2020b), and that is an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated image inputs, or the cited InceptionV1 neuron.
No language models or transformer MLP neuron response mixtures.
Does not test superposition or capacity pressure as a cause of polysemanticity.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
Does not compare activation functions or training regimes for polysemanticity, or test performance costs of reducing it.
Does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons share a feature or are misread generalizations.
It compares visualization sampling choices and a coherence-rating task, but does not test whether those choices change which neurons count as polysemantic.

rows.subject: 22 user study participants judging AlexNet visualizations
rows.operation_detail: Participants chose which of two visualizations showed a coherent left-to-right transition; one was shuffled.
rows.measure: Participant accuracy on identifying the coherent visualization
rows.value: PCA visualizations gave significantly better continuity perception: F(1,21)=34.50, p<.001; exact accuracy values not stated in text
rows.uncertainty: p<.001; standard errors plotted in Figure 7
rows.note: This measures interpretability of basis visualizations, not whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs.

rows.subject: 22 user study participants judging AlexNet visualizations
rows.operation_detail: Rated coherent transitions in neuron and PCA visualizations from fully connected layers.
rows.measure: Participant accuracy on identifying the coherent visualization
rows.value: PCA advantage: F(1,21)=32.91, p<.001; exact accuracy values not stated in text
rows.note: The study reports an interpretability difference, not a measure of polysemantic responses.

rows.subject: 22 user study participants judging AlexNet visualizations
rows.operation_detail: Rated coherent transitions in neuron and PCA visualizations from convolutional layers.
rows.measure: Participant accuracy on identifying the coherent visualization
rows.value: PCA advantage: F(1,21)=9.32, p<.001; exact accuracy values not stated in text
rows.note: The study reports an interpretability difference, not a measure of polysemantic responses.
rows.check: The text reports F(1,21)=9.32 with p<.001. That F with those degrees of freedom gives roughly p≈.006, so the value is transcribed correctly but the paper's p looks overstated.

rows.value: F(2,42)=4.01, p<.05; authors say the depth effect is difficult to interpret

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared cumulative explained variance for ordered PCA components and neurons.
rows.measure: Number of basis vectors needed to explain activation variance
rows.value: 42 PCs
rows.note: The paper reports the count comparison directly and says similar concentration trends occur in every layer.

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Cumulatively ablated activation-space PCs or neurons in descending explained-variance order and measured validation accuracy.
rows.measure: ImageNet top-1 validation accuracy after ablation
rows.baseline: Original accuracy; numerical value not stated
rows.value: Ablating high-variance neurons was more damaging than ablating high-variance PCs
rows.note: The text explicitly identifies conv1 as the exception to the general pattern.
rows.check: The 'reversed' state is relative to the study's own PCA-vs-neuron pattern, not to any claim version. Under these rules an unlinked row's state should be cannot_determine.

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Cumulatively ablated activation-space PCs or neurons in descending explained-variance order and measured validation accuracy.
rows.measure: ImageNet top-1 validation accuracy after ablation
rows.baseline: Original accuracy; numerical value not stated
rows.value: Accuracy generally degraded faster when high-variance PCs were ablated than when high-variance neurons were ablated
rows.note: The authors describe the general pattern as applying with the exception of conv1.

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Cumulatively ablated activation-space PCs or neurons in descending explained-variance order and measured validation accuracy.
rows.measure: ImageNet top-1 validation accuracy after ablation
rows.baseline: Original accuracy; numerical value not stated
rows.value: For approximately the first 50 high-variance PCs, accuracy degraded faster than with neuron ablation; beyond that point, neuron ablation was more damaging
rows.note: The authors hypothesize the later reversal relates to the heavier-tailed eigenspectra in these layers.
rows.check: The 'partial' state is relative to the study's own PCA-vs-neuron pattern, not to a claim version. It is the study's method compared against neurons.

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared visualizations of neuron and PCA basis vectors across layers.
rows.measure: Semantic interpretability of natural-image visualizations
rows.value: Neuron visualizations appeared semantically meaningless; the paper says the neuron basis becomes quite uninterpretable after conv1
rows.note: This is an explicit qualitative judgment about visualizations, not a test of unrelated response categories.
rows.check: Closest row to V1, but 'semantically meaningless' neuron visualizations are not shown to mix unrelated concepts. Correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared visualizations sampled between activation minimum and maximum with visualizations sampled between the first and ninety-ninth percentiles.
rows.measure: Qualitative distinctness and interpretability of visualizations
rows.value: Minimum-to-maximum sampling produced visualizations that demonstrated the feature more distinctly; authors report this conclusion after examining several basis vectors from each layer
rows.note: This shows a visualization sampling choice affects apparent feature distinctness, but does not count polysemantic neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction cites polysemanticity (Olah et al. 2020b) as one reason neurons are a poor basis. 'discusses' fits.

tranche.reason: The paper compares PCA and neuron bases on explained variance, ablation and human coherence ratings. It does not measure whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, so it tests no version.

source_check.notes: Only R16 was checked, as the pack listed. The text states the 80% fc1 comparison: first 42 PCs vs the 2782 highest-variance neurons, in PyTorch's ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet. Low neuron interpretability in the user study is a coherence measure, not a polysemanticity measure.
